title: Managing Medical Conditions: Hypothermia, Heat Exhaustion & Dehydration
description: Causes, symptoms and treatment of hypothermia, heat exhaustion and dehydration, plus managing conditions in a.
content_html:
Environmental and Fluid-Related Conditions in Sport

Alongside the conditions covered in earlier lessons, sports performers are also at risk from conditions caused by the external environment and inadequate hydration. Hypothermia, heat exhaustion and dehydration are all examinable under Topic Area 5 of R180. Each is directly linked to the extrinsic factors studied in Topic Area 1, particularly weather and temperature conditions.

Hypothermia: Causes and Symptoms

Hypothermia occurs when the body's core temperature drops below 35 degrees Celsius. In sport, the two key causes are: the body losing heat faster than it can produce it in cold conditions (body temperature drops below 35°C) and prolonged exposure to cold or wet conditions — for example, a cross-country runner in rain and wind, an open-water swimmer or a cyclist descending a mountain. Inadequate clothing (1.1.4) significantly increases this risk.

The five symptoms of hypothermia listed in the specification are: shivering (the body's automatic attempt to generate heat through muscle activity), blue lips or skin (cyanosis — reduced blood flow to the periphery as the body prioritises core organs), slurred speech (cold affects neuromuscular coordination), tiredness or confusion (the brain functions less effectively as core temperature falls) and slow breathing (respiratory rate drops as metabolism slows in the cold).

Hypothermia: Treatment

Treatment for hypothermia involves gently warming the performer. The two specification treatments are: remove wet clothing and wrap in blankets, covering the head (wet clothing conducts heat away from the body rapidly, so removal and insulation are the first priority — covering the head is important because significant heat loss occurs through the scalp) and give a warm, sugary, non-alcoholic drink (warm fluids raise core temperature from the inside; sugar provides a rapid energy source; alcohol must be avoided as it causes blood vessels near the skin to dilate, actually increasing heat loss).

Key Fact

Hypothermia must NOT be treated with a hot bath, hot water bottle, or by rubbing the body parts — these cause rapid vasodilation that can send cold blood from the periphery to the core, causing cardiac complications. Warming must be gradual and gentle.

Heat Exhaustion: Causes and Symptoms

Heat exhaustion occurs when the body overheats, typically with a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or above. Three causes are listed: body temperature reaching 38°C or above (the body's thermoregulatory mechanisms begin to fail), strenuous physical activity (generating high levels of internal heat that the body cannot dissipate fast enough) and not enough water intake (without adequate fluid, sweating — the primary cooling mechanism — is impaired). Hot, humid environments make heat exhaustion more likely because high humidity prevents sweat from evaporating effectively.

The five symptoms of heat exhaustion are: excessive sweating (the body's cooling attempt, which causes significant fluid loss), headache or dizziness (dehydration and reduced blood pressure to the brain), being very thirsty (the body signals its fluid deficit), feeling or being sick (nausea and vomiting caused by dehydration and heat stress on the gastrointestinal system) and rapid pulse and/or rapid breathing (the cardiovascular system working harder to circulate blood and transfer heat to the skin).

Heat Exhaustion: Treatment

Treatment for heat exhaustion is straightforward and must be applied quickly before the condition deteriorates into heatstroke (a life-threatening emergency). The two specification treatments are: move the performer to a cool place and cool their skin — for example, move them into the shade or an air-conditioned area, loosen clothing, apply cool damp cloths to the skin or use a fan — and get them to drink plenty of water to replace the fluid lost through sweating. If the performer does not improve within 30 minutes or becomes confused or loses consciousness, call 999.

Key Fact

Hypothermia: core body temperature below 35°C. Heat exhaustion: body temperature of 38°C or above. These are the threshold temperatures specified by the specification and must be learned precisely.

Dehydration: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment

Dehydration is caused by loss of bodily fluids — primarily through sweating during exercise — that are not adequately replaced. In sport, dehydration impairs thermoregulation, reduces blood volume, slows reaction times and decreases strength and aerobic capacity. There is a direct link between dehydration and both diabetes (5.2) — because high blood sugar causes the kidneys to excrete more water — and heat exhaustion, since dehydration prevents effective sweating.

The four symptoms of dehydration are: feeling thirsty (thirst is actually a late sign — by the time you feel thirsty, performance is already impaired), fatigue (reduced blood volume means less oxygen delivered to muscles), dark yellow urine and infrequent urination (the kidneys conserve water by concentrating urine — pale urine indicates good hydration; dark urine indicates dehydration) and dry mouth or lips (reduced saliva production as the body conserves fluid). Treatment is simple: drink plenty of water as the first step, with rehydration sachets (oral rehydration salts) used in cases of significant fluid and electrolyte loss to restore the correct balance of water and minerals.

The best approach to dehydration in sport is prevention. Performers should hydrate well before training, drink regularly during activity (approximately 150–250 ml every 15–20 minutes in moderate conditions, more in heat), and continue rehydrating after training. Coaches should build regular drink breaks into sessions and ensure water is always available at training venues. Monitoring urine colour is a practical and reliable way for performers to self-assess hydration status. Diabetic performers must be especially vigilant as high blood sugar can cause increased urination (polyuria), accelerating dehydration.

The specification explicitly links weather and temperature conditions (1.1.3) to medical risk. Cold, wet weather increases hypothermia risk — appropriate clothing (1.1.4) and a warm-up that raises core temperature (Topic Area 2) both mitigate this. Hot, humid conditions increase heat exhaustion and dehydration risk — session scheduling, shade, cooling zones and mandatory hydration breaks are control measures identified in a risk assessment. Coaches should always check weather forecasts before outdoor sessions and have a written protocol for extreme conditions as part of their Emergency Action Plan.
exam_tip_html: For questions on hypothermia, always include the 'do nots' — no hot bath, no hot water bottle, do not rub body parts. These are specific to the specification and earn marks. For dehydration questions, remember that thirst is a late sign of dehydration, not an early warning — performers should drink before they feel thirsty. For any 'compare' question on these three conditions, the distinguishing factor is temperature: hypothermia (below 35°C, cold cause), heat exhaustion (38°C or above, hot cause), dehydration (fluid loss, relevant in both hot and cold conditions).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hypothermia (below 35°C) is treated by removing wet clothing, wrapping in blankets covering the head and giving a warm sugary non-alcoholic drink; never use a hot bath, hot water bottle or rub body parts.
  • Heat exhaustion (38°C or above) is caused by strenuous activity, hot conditions and insufficient fluid intake; treat by moving to a cool place, cooling the skin and drinking plenty of water.
  • Dehydration is caused by fluid loss during exercise and is treated with water and rehydration sachets; symptoms include thirst, fatigue, dark yellow urine and dry mouth, and it is directly linked to heat exhaustion and diabetes.

glossary_terms.definition: A dangerous drop in core body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius caused by prolonged exposure to cold or wet conditions.
A condition caused by overheating during strenuous activity or in hot environments, characterised by heavy sweating, dizziness and rapid pulse.
A condition caused by loss of bodily fluids that are not replaced, impairing physical and cognitive performance.
Oral rehydration salts dissolved in water, used to restore the correct balance of fluid and electrolytes after significant fluid loss.

practice_questions.text:
At what core body temperature does hypothermia begin?
A) Below 37°C
B) Below 36°C
C) Below 35°C
D) Below 34°C
State two symptoms of heat exhaustion.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: excessive sweating / headache or dizziness / being very thirsty / feeling or being sick / rapid pulse and/or rapid breathing. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a performer suffering from hypothermia should not be warmed using a hot bath or hot water bottle.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Basic point (1 mark): a hot bath or hot water bottle must not be used to treat hypothermia. Reason (2 marks): rapid heat causes blood vessels near the skin surface to dilate (vasodilate) suddenly. Further development (3 marks): this causes cold blood from the periphery — the arms, legs and skin surface — to rush back to the core all at once, which can cause dangerous cardiac complications and a sudden further drop in core temperature. Warming must therefore be gradual and gentle. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the causes and treatment of dehydration in sport. Give an example of when rehydration sachets would be more appropriate than water alone.
practice_questions.marks: Cause (1 mark): dehydration is caused by loss of bodily fluids — primarily through sweating during exercise — that are not replaced. Treatment (2 marks): drink plenty of water as the first-line treatment (1 mark); use rehydration sachets to restore fluid and electrolyte balance in cases of significant fluid loss (1 mark). Example (1 mark): rehydration sachets would be more appropriate than water alone after a marathon or long-distance endurance event where significant sweating has caused both fluid and electrolyte depletion — replacing water alone without electrolytes can dilute blood sodium and cause hyponatraemia. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A junior football team trains on an exposed pitch on a cold, wet January afternoon. The coach notices that two players are showing signs of hypothermia, and later in the session a third player complains of feeling thirsty and dizzy.

Discuss how the coach should respond to these three players and what measures should be in place to prevent these conditions occurring at future sessions.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A structured discussion covering correct treatment for both hypothermia (remove wet clothing, wrap in blankets covering head, warm non-alcoholic sugary drink, avoid hot bath / hot water bottle / rubbing) and dehydration/possible heat exhaustion (drink water, rest, move to shelter). Prevention discussed with at least two specific measures for future sessions — e.g. mandatory warm kit policy, weather checks before training, drink breaks built into the session plan, risk assessment for cold-weather training. At least one contrast — e.g. the session plan alone cannot prevent all environmental conditions, but an Emergency Action Plan ensures the response is immediate when incidents occur.
Secure (3–4 marks): Both conditions addressed with treatment and some prevention.
Developing (2 marks): One condition treated adequately, prevention vague.
Emerging (1 mark): One relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Three environmental medical conditions — hypothermia, heat exhaustion and dehydration — are all linked to external factors that coaches can influence through planning and preparation.

Evaluate the extent to which effective planning and risk assessment by a coach can prevent these three conditions from occurring during outdoor sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A well-structured evaluation arguing that planning reduces risk significantly — risk assessments identify weather hazards, appropriate clothing policies prevent hypothermia, mandatory hydration breaks and water provision prevent dehydration, session scheduling in cooler periods reduces heat exhaustion risk, and Emergency Action Plans ensure rapid response when conditions deteriorate. Counter-arguments then challenge the extent of control: weather is unpredictable, performers arrive with pre-existing dehydration or inadequate kit, coaches cannot control individual hydration habits, and some environmental conditions deteriorate suddenly during a session. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached about what planning can realistically achieve versus what remains outside the coach's control.
Secure (5–6 marks): Arguments on both sides with some application to the scenario and a partial judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Mainly lists preventive measures without counter-argument or clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which symptom is specifically associated with hypothermia but NOT heat exhaustion?
Which of the following is the correct treatment for heat exhaustion?
options: Move to a cool place, cool the skin and drink plenty of water
Wrap in blankets and give a warm sugary drink
Apply a hot water bottle to warm the performer
Give rehydration sachets and place in a hot bath

knowledge_checks.q: A performer who is dehydrated may produce _____ urine, which is a practical sign that more fluid is needed.
The specification states that hypothermia must NOT be treated by using a hot bath, hot water bottle, or by _____ the affected body parts.
Match each condition to its primary cause.
right: Loss of bodily fluids not replaced during exercise
Body temperature of 38°C or above due to strenuous activity or hot environment
Core body temperature drops below 35°C due to prolonged cold or wet exposure

flashcard_questions.q: At what core temperature does hypothermia begin?
flashcard_questions.a: Hypothermia begins when the body's core temperature drops below 35 degrees Celsius, typically due to prolonged cold or wet exposure.

flashcard_questions.q: State the five symptoms of hypothermia.
flashcard_questions.a: Shivering, blue lips or skin, slurred speech, tiredness or confusion, and slow breathing are the five specification symptoms of hypothermia.

flashcard_questions.q: Why should a hypothermic performer's head be covered when wrapped in blankets?
flashcard_questions.a: Significant heat loss occurs through the scalp, so covering the head helps retain body heat and aids gradual rewarming of the core.

flashcard_questions.q: Why should alcohol not be given to a hypothermic performer?
flashcard_questions.a: Alcohol causes peripheral blood vessels to dilate, increasing heat loss from the skin surface and making the core temperature fall further.

flashcard_questions.q: What body temperature marks the onset of heat exhaustion?
flashcard_questions.a: Heat exhaustion is associated with a body temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or above, combined with strenuous activity or hot conditions.

flashcard_questions.q: State two causes of heat exhaustion.
flashcard_questions.a: Heat exhaustion is caused by strenuous physical activity generating excessive heat and insufficient water intake impairing the body's cooling mechanisms.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the immediate treatment for heat exhaustion?
flashcard_questions.a: Move the performer to a cool place and cool their skin, then ensure they drink plenty of water to replace fluid lost through sweating.
Dehydration is caused by the loss of bodily fluids through sweating during exercise that are not adequately replaced before, during or after activity.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is dark yellow urine a sign of dehydration?
flashcard_questions.a: When dehydrated, the kidneys conserve water by producing less, more concentrated urine, which appears dark yellow rather than pale straw-coloured.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are rehydration sachets used rather than water alone after severe dehydration?
flashcard_questions.a: Rehydration sachets contain oral rehydration salts that replace both water and electrolytes lost in sweat, restoring the correct fluid and mineral balance.

flashcard_questions.q: How is dehydration directly linked to diabetes?
flashcard_questions.a: High blood sugar in diabetes causes the kidneys to excrete more water through urine (polyuria), significantly accelerating fluid loss and dehydration.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the link between dehydration and heat exhaustion?
flashcard_questions.a: Dehydration impairs sweating, which is the body's primary cooling mechanism, making heat exhaustion more likely and more severe during exercise in the heat.
